A weaker USD would also be expected. However, she notes that for energy-importing FX currencies, a more sustainable turnaround would also require confirmation of softer US data and a more clearly dovish Fed stance.

headline: ECB hikes 25bp in symbolic move to signal inflation commitment, but ANZ warns it will exacerbate growth headwinds
reasoning: The ECB raised rates by 25 basis points, marking its first hike since 2023 and the first G7 central bank to hike in 2026 since the Iran conflict erupted. ANZ economist Henry Russell characterises the move as largely symbolic, designed to communicate commitment to the inflation target rather than being warranted by recent data. The hike is not expected to materially alter the near-term inflation path but is seen as likely to worsen existing headwinds to growth and the labour market.
quote: As expected, the ECB hiked 25 basis points today. And what we would categorise is a largely symbolic move that was more about communicating the ECB's commitment to its inflation target than necessarily being warranted by the evolution of data in recent months. Today's rate hike will do little to alter the near term path for inflation. But in our view, it will exacerbate existing headwinds to both growth and the labour market.

headline: Australian sheep and lamb sector outlook remains strong as Australia dominates global supply, though consumer price resistance is a risk
reasoning: Australia is the dominant global supplier of sheep and lamb, with no competing production volumes large enough to distort the market. Seasonal conditions are improving, and competition between restockers and processors is expected to support prices. The sector benefits from strong demand in the US as a premium market and in China, though Middle East and North African markets have been slower due to trade disruptions. Consumer resistance at retail shelf prices — particularly relative to cheaper proteins like chicken — is flagged as the key demand moderator to watch.
quote: Sheep's a bit more interesting because it's not as big a market as the beef market is. And there's probably a point at which consumers will resist the prices on the shelf. It's a big market for us into the US, but it's a premium market over there... We are a dominant global supplier of this product. There is really no production volume that would distort that market for Australia. And again, as long as seasonal conditions are good in Australia and they are improving from where we had been. So again, you've got that restocker breeder retention issue competing against the processes who will be looking for product to satisfy other market opportunities that are out there. That all bodes well for prices.

headline: ANZ agribusiness head sees continued upside for Australian beef prices driven by US herd shortage and strong export demand
reasoning: Australian beef prices experienced a seasonal autumn dip as dry conditions in southern Queensland and northern NSW pushed cattle to market, but recent rains have improved the desire to hold stock. The key medium-term driver is the US herd shortfall and difficult domestic conditions in America, which limits US export competition in key markets like Japan and Korea. With Australia rebuilding its herd and strong export demand intact, Bennett argues there is a solid case for beef prices to continue rising. China tariff timing has also prompted pre-tariff forward buying, adding near-term demand support.
quote: The real driver for the medium outlook on cattle is the US herd lull and the difficult conditions still being experienced in America. And even the incentive to rebuild that herd in some respects, I would say as well. So whilst that looks like a long haul, it really keeps the US from being as dominant an exporter into some of our key competing markets. And so as Australia starts to rebuild its herd a little and has the capacity to hold on and with that strong export demand, there is a decent argument to think beef prices will continue to rise.

headline: US core CPI signals weak demand with energy price shock not flowing through to broader economy
reasoning: ANZ Head of G3 Economics Brian Martin notes that while headline CPI rose 0.5% in May, core inflation was only 0.2%, and a sub-measure excluding shelter, used cars and trucks rose just 0.1% — its lowest in a year. He interprets this as evidence that demand in the economy is weak, with businesses unable to pass on higher energy costs and margins being compressed. Consumers are described as stretched, with an affordability crisis affecting many US households not benefiting from wealth effects of the stock market.
quote: When you look at some of the core measures within the core measure, one which excludes shelter used cars and trucks, that rose 0.1% in the month, which matched its lowest rating in the past year. And I think what the inflation data are telling us is that demand in the economy is weak. Demand are having difficulty pushing up prices, margins are being compressed. And consumers, we know, are stretched. There is an affordability crisis in the United States for many households that aren't benefiting from the wealth effects of the stock market.

headline: Indonesia tightening nickel supply rules — mining quota cut 30-35%, annual permit system reinstated — set to contract production by over 200,000 tonnes for first time since 2020
reasoning: ANZ Commodities Strategist Sunny Kamari explains that Indonesia, which accounts for 60-70% of global nickel production, has moved aggressively to tighten supply controls in 2025. From February, the government reduced the mining quota to 260-270 million tonnes from 379 million tonnes — a net 30-35% decline — and scrapped the multi-year permit system in favour of strict annual quota reviews, giving the government greater control and creating investment uncertainty. In April, the benchmark nickel ore price methodology was changed to also factor in byproduct values, adding ~US$4,500/tonne to costs particularly for HPAL processors. Corporate decisions, including Singswan asking NPI producers to cut output 10%, are reinforcing the supply squeeze. Together these changes are expected to see Indonesian production contract by over 200,000 tonnes for the first time since 2020.
quote: Indonesia is the largest producer of nickel, as I mentioned, and the annual production growth has been nearly, you know, nearly 30 percent over the last one decade. But these regulatory changes will see Indonesian production contracting by over 200,000 tons for the first time since 2020. So we expect nickel refined output to fall by 60,000 tons, which will push the global market into a smaller deficit. So therefore we expect, you know, prices to find a former floor above 17,000 dollars per ton this year.
